passage: Zanele arrived at the library meeting room in Hamburg at half past ten. The project group had started at ten sharp. Selin looked at the clock, then at Zanele, and said only, "We've begun the first section." Back home in Durban, ten o'clock meant people drifted in by eleven and nobody minded. Here, three classmates who had waited exchanged a look. Zanele's face went hot, and Zanele stayed to the end without a word. Afterwards Zanele said, "I didn't understand how strict the clock is here. I'm sorry." Selin nodded. "If you're running late, send a message before, even five minutes." Zanele set the alarm fifteen minutes early, and the next week arrived first.

qa.q: How late was Zanele to the meeting?
qa.a: Zanele arrived at half past ten for a group that had started at ten sharp.

qa.q: How did Zanele feel when Selin looked at the clock?
qa.a: Embarrassed and worried about seeming unreliable; the face went hot.

qa.q: What could Zanele do whenever running late in future?
qa.a: Send a message before, even for five minutes, and leave earlier.

qa.q: How might Selin and the classmates have seen the late arrival?
qa.a: As a lack of respect for their time, since they had waited from ten, though Zanele meant no offence.

grounding: A student used to flexible timings arrives half an hour late in a strict-time setting, then learns the local clock and to message ahead.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: At the engineering office in Frankfurt, the induction started at nine. Saurabh, an intern from Jaipur, walked in at half past nine, smiling and apologising about the tram. Vasudha, the HR coordinator, was already handing badges to the others. "We began at nine," Vasudha said evenly. "Here, arriving on time means being there before the start." Saurabh's smile faded. Back home, half an hour late for a family gathering hardly counted. "I didn't know," Saurabh said. "Could you tell me what I missed, and how to let you know if something delays me?" Vasudha handed over the printout and wrote a phone number at the top. "Call before, not after." Next morning Saurabh was in the lobby at ten to nine.

qa.q: What time did the induction start?
qa.a: The induction started at nine.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when the smile faded?
qa.a: Embarrassed and uneasy, realising that being late had been taken seriously.

qa.q: What small steps could Saurabh take to avoid offence?
qa.a: Arrive before the start and call ahead if something delays the journey.

qa.q: How does Vasudha see arriving on time?
qa.a: As being there before the start, which respects everyone's schedule.

grounding: A student used to flexible timings arrives late at a strict-time workplace and learns to arrive early and tell people ahead.

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage:
Supervisor's note, biology lab, Zurich exchange programme, week 2.
Noor arrived at Monday's group meeting at 9:32 for a 9:00 start, smiling, with coffee. The room had already moved on to the second item. Two of the local students exchanged a look, and afterwards one of them asked me, quietly, whether Noor could be trusted with the shared incubator schedule. I asked Noor to stay back. Noor looked genuinely puzzled: at home, Noor said, a nine o'clock meeting usually begins when the senior arrives. When I explained that here half an hour late reads as not caring, Noor went red and went very quiet.
Shankar, our technician, who came from Chennai years ago, offered a tip: set the watch ten minutes fast and message the group if the tram is late. On Thursday the tram was late. At 8:52 the group got Noor's message: "Tram stuck, arriving 9:07, sorry." Nobody minded at all.

qa.q: What time did Noor arrive at Monday's meeting?
qa.a: Noor arrived at 9:32 for a 9:00 start.

qa.q: How did Noor feel on learning how the lateness was seen?
qa.a: Noor was puzzled at first and then embarrassed, going red and very quiet.

qa.q: Which two tips from Shankar helped, and why?
qa.a: Setting the watch ten minutes fast and messaging the group when late; together they respect the local clock and show care even when delays happen.

qa.q: How did the local students see Noor's late arrival?
qa.a: They took it as a sign Noor might be unreliable, even wondering whether Noor could be trusted with the incubator schedule.

grounding: It illustrates a student used to flexible timings who arrives half an hour late in a strict-time culture, is seen as unreliable, and learns to tell people ahead.

passage:
Tuesday, Berlin
I want to crawl under the duvet. Our project group met at the library at 4. I left the hostel at 4, because at home 4 means around 4:30 and everyone knows it. I walked in at 4:31 and they had already split the work. Jonas said, "We thought you weren't coming." Not angry, just flat. Somebody had taken my section. I spent the whole meeting feeling like the unreliable Indian girl, which is worse than being angry.
Afterwards Lakshmi di, who's in her second year here, walked me to the tram. She said she did the exact same thing in her first month and a professor stopped talking until she sat down. Her rule: in Germany, 4 means 3:55. And if you're even five minutes late, message.
So: new alarm, 3:40, labelled GERMAN FOUR. Tomorrow I'm going to ask for my section back. Nandini, the new punctual version.

qa.q: When did Nandini walk into the library meeting?
How did Nandini feel during the meeting, and why?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and small, like the unreliable girl, because the group had already split the work and someone had taken her section.

qa.q: What rule did Lakshmi di share, and why is it useful?
qa.a: In Germany 4 means 3:55, and message if even five minutes late; it helps Nandini match the local sense of time and avoid offence.

qa.q: How might Jonas have seen Nandini's late arrival?
qa.a: Jonas probably read it as not caring about the group, and felt unsure whether to count on her, which is why he said they thought she wasn't coming.

grounding: It illustrates a student used to flexible timings who arrives thirty minutes late in a strict-time setting, is seen as unreliable, and learns the local clock.

Sonali: two things. email the prof today, short sorry, no excuses. and from now on, if you'll be even 5 mins late, message before

subtopic: Global cultures: eye contact, personal space, directness and time
passage: The local bus from Kherwadi stopped at every tea stall, and Naveen didn't mind; back home, a meeting at ten meant somewhere near eleven. He reached the seed-trial farm at ten-thirty, sweating, pickle still on his fingers. Siddharth was waiting at the gate, face tight. "She started at ten sharp," he whispered. "Dr. Lena from the Dutch team asked twice where you were. Then she wrote something in her notebook." Inside, Dr. Lena gave Naveen a polite nod and handed the soil samples to Siddharth instead. Naveen's ears burned. That evening, on the bench at the bus stop, Siddharth explained that where she came from, half an hour late meant you did not care. Naveen had not meant that at all. The next week the bus broke down near the canal. At 9:40 he sent a message: "Bus stuck, reaching by 10:20, very sorry." Dr. Lena replied, "Thank you for telling me. We will start with the maps."

qa.q: What time did Naveen reach the seed-trial farm the first time?
qa.a: He reached the seed-trial farm at ten-thirty, sweating, with pickle still on his fingers.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when Dr. Lena handed the soil samples to Siddharth instead?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt; his ears burned because he could see she now doubted he could be relied on, though he had meant no disrespect.

qa.q: What small step helped Naveen the second time he was running late?
qa.a: He sent a message twenty minutes before the start with a new arrival time and an apology, so Dr. Lena could plan instead of wondering whether he cared.

qa.q: How might Dr. Lena have seen Naveen's first late arrival?
qa.a: In her way of working, turning up half an hour late without a word looked like not caring about the work, so she gave the task to Siddharth.

grounding: Shows a student used to loose timings arriving half an hour late to a strict-time meeting, being judged unreliable, and then warning ahead the next time.
